subject: English
description: Comma, semicolon, colon, apostrophe, quotation marks — usage rules

options.option_text: He bought apples oranges and pears.
He bought apples, oranges, and pears.
He bought, apples oranges, and pears.
He, bought apples oranges and pears.

questions.explanation: Series rule — separate items in a list with commas. The 'Oxford / serial' comma before 'and' (in 'apples, oranges, and pears') is preferred in American English; British English often omits it but never inconsistently. Avoid commas after the verb ('bought,') unless setting off an interrupting phrase. Listing example: 'I want eggs, bread, and milk.' The Oxford comma can also disambiguate — 'I love my parents, Lady Gaga, and Humpty Dumpty' vs 'I love my parents, Lady Gaga and Humpty Dumpty' (the latter implies they ARE her parents).

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the apostrophe correctly?
questions.explanation: ITS — possessive (no apostrophe; like 'his', 'her'). IT'S — contraction of 'it is' or 'it has'. So 'the dog wagged ITS tail' (possessive). Apostrophe rules: (1) singular noun + 's ('John's car'); (2) plural noun ending in 's' + ' ('dogs' tails'); (3) plural not ending in 's' + 's ('children's books'). Never use apostrophe to make plurals (NOT 'apple's' for two apples — write 'apples').

questions.stem: Identify the SENTENCE that correctly uses a SEMICOLON:

options.option_text: She loves; tea, coffee and milk.
He travelled extensively; he visited Paris, Rome, and Tokyo.
I went to the; market yesterday.

questions.explanation: Semicolon (;) connects two independent (complete) clauses that are closely related — 'He travelled extensively; he visited Paris...' Both halves can stand alone as sentences. Stronger than a comma but weaker than a full stop. Also used to separate items in a list when the items themselves contain commas — 'We invited Anil, my brother; Beena, my colleague; and Chetan, my friend.' Don't use semicolons after subject ('She loves;') or before adjective ('the book is;').
questions.subject: English

options.option_text: Three nations attended: India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh.

questions.explanation: COLON (:) introduces a list, an explanation, an example, or a quotation. The text BEFORE the colon should stand as a complete clause. Correct: 'Three nations attended: India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh.' (the first part is a complete clause). Don't break the verb-object link with a colon — 'She bought: apples' is wrong. Other valid uses: time (10:30), ratio (3:5), Bible references (John 3:16), titles ('The book: a sequel').
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Which sentence handles QUOTATION MARKS correctly (American convention)?
questions.explanation: American convention — comma before opening quote; period (or comma) inside the closing quote (always). 'She said, "I am tired."' British convention puts logical punctuation: only marks belonging to the original quoted sentence go inside; otherwise outside. Most exam papers in India follow British convention but accept either. ALWAYS capitalise the first word of a complete quoted sentence: ' "I am tired," she said.'
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Pick the sentence with the correct usage of the EM-DASH:

options.option_text: Three friends—Aman, Bina, Chetan—came to visit.

questions.explanation: Em-dash (—) — sets off a parenthetical phrase MORE EMPHATICALLY than commas or parentheses. 'Three friends—Aman, Bina, Chetan—came to visit.' Replaces commas / brackets when you want the interrupting phrase to stand out. Don't break inseparable elements (subject-verb or verb-object) with em-dashes. Hyphen (-) for compound words (well-known); en-dash (–) for ranges (1990–2020). On the keyboard, the em-dash is two hyphens or Alt+0151 / Option-Shift-Hyphen on Mac.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Identify the correctly punctuated sentence with hyphenation:

options.option_text: He is a well known scientist.
He is a well-known scientist (compound modifier before noun).

questions.explanation: Hyphen joins compound modifiers BEFORE a noun: 'a well-known scientist'. AFTER a verb (predicative position), no hyphen is needed: 'The scientist is well known'. Other examples: 'a state-of-the-art lab' but 'the lab is state of the art'. Compound nouns generally take hyphens (mother-in-law, brother-in-law). Numbers — hyphenated when written: 'twenty-one'. Prefixes — usually no hyphen ('pre-school' vs 'preschool' is style-dependent).
